concepts.title: Measuring Heights Using Parallel Lines
concepts.one_liner: Distances in the world can be measured from a single image using three vanishing points or the horizon line and one vanishing point.
concepts.content: Distances in the world can be measured from a single image without using camera calibration or the projection matrix. This can be achieved using three vanishing points, or just the horizon line and one vanishing point. For a deeper analysis, the reader is referred to the thesis of A. Criminisi.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept introduces the possibility of performing 3D measurements directly from 2D images by leveraging geometric properties like vanishing points and the horizon, bypassing the need for complex camera calibration.
concepts.recap_md:
- Measurements can be made from a single image using vanishing points and the horizon line.
- This approach avoids the requirement for camera calibration or projection matrices.

concepts.title: Cross-Ratio
concepts.one_liner: The cross-ratio of four collinear points is a specific ratio of the Euclidean distances between them.
concepts.content:
The cross-ratio of four collinear points is defined by the expression:
$$CR \left( \mathbf{P}_1,\mathbf{P}_2,\mathbf{P}_3,\mathbf{P}_4 \right) 
= 
\frac{\left| \mathbf{P}_3 -\mathbf{P}_1 \right| \left|\mathbf{P}_4 -\mathbf{P}_2 \right|}
{\left| \mathbf{P}_3 -\mathbf{P}_2 \right| \left|\mathbf{P}_4 -\mathbf{P}_1 \right|}$$
where $\left| \mathbf{P}_i -\mathbf{P}_j \right|$ is the euclidean distance between points $\mathbf{P}_i$ and $\mathbf{P}_j$, using heterogeneous coordinates.

[FIGURE:c3a83d33f5a7a7b5 | A diagram showing four collinear points labeled $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, and $P_4$ arranged along a single pink line. The points are spaced out from bottom-left to top-right to illustrate the geometric...]
concepts.motivation_md: The cross-ratio is a fundamental quantity in projective geometry because it remains invariant under projective transformations, allowing for consistent measurements across different perspectives.
concepts.recap_md:
- It is defined for four collinear points using their Euclidean distances.
- The formula is $CR = \frac{|P_3-P_1||P_4-P_2|}{|P_3-P_2||P_4-P_1|}$.

concepts.title: Cross-Ratio Invariance
concepts.one_liner: The cross-ratio is a projective invariant, meaning it remains unchanged when points are related by a projective transformation.
concepts.content:
The cross-ratio is considered the most important projective invariant. Two sets of points $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$ related by a projective transformation have the same cross-ratio, regardless of the choice of origin $\mathbf{O}$ or scale factor. That is:
$$CR(\mathbf{P}_1,\mathbf{P}_2,\mathbf{P}_3,\mathbf{P}_4) = CR(\mathbf{Q}_1,\mathbf{Q}_2,\mathbf{Q}_3,\mathbf{Q}_4)$$

(see figure: The set of points $\mathbf{P}$ are related to the points $\mathbf{Q}$ (and $\mathbf{R}$) by the cross-ratio. The point $\mathbf{R}_1$ is in infinity because the line connecting the points...)
concepts.motivation_md: Invariance is a powerful property in computer vision; it allows us to relate measurements in a distorted image back to the original 3D scene without knowing the specific camera parameters.
concepts.recap_md:
- The cross-ratio is the most important projective invariant.
- It remains constant across projective transformations, independent of origin or scale.

slots.motivation: Invariance is a powerful property in computer vision; it allows us to relate measurements in a distorted image back to the original 3D scene without knowing the specific camera parameters.
slots.key_passage:
- The cross-ratio is the most important projective invariant.
- It remains constant across projective transformations, independent of origin or scale.

concepts.title: Cross-Ratio with Points at Infinity
concepts.one_liner: When one point in a cross-ratio is at infinity, the expression simplifies as terms containing that point cancel out.
concepts.content:
(see figure: The set of points $\mathbf{P}$ are related to the points $\mathbf{Q}$ (and $\mathbf{R}$) by the cross-ratio. The point $\mathbf{R}_1$ is in infinity because the line connecting the points...)

When one of the points is at infinity, all the terms that contain that point are cancelled out (this can also be seen by taking a limit). In the case of the points $\mathbf{R}$ from the figure, where $\mathbf{R}_1$ is at infinity, the cross-ratio becomes:
$$CR(\mathbf{R}_1,\mathbf{R}_2,\mathbf{R}_3,\mathbf{R}_4) = 
\frac{\left| \mathbf{R}_4 -\mathbf{R}_2 \right| } 
{ \left| \mathbf{R}_3 -\mathbf{R}_2 \right|}$$
This value is equal to the cross-ratio of the corresponding points $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$.
concepts.motivation_md: In perspective views, parallel lines meet at vanishing points (points at infinity). This simplification allows us to calculate cross-ratios using vanishing points, which is essential for measuring heights in images.
concepts.recap_md:
- Points at infinity simplify the cross-ratio formula by canceling out associated terms.
- For $\mathbf{R}_1$ at infinity, the ratio reduces to $\frac{|R_4-R_2|}{|R_3-R_2|}$.

concepts.title: Ordering in Cross-Ratio Calculation
concepts.one_liner: The numerical value of a cross-ratio depends on the specific order in which the four points are considered.
concepts.content: The order in which these points are considered matters in the calculation. There are $4!=24$ possible orderings resulting in six different values. If two sets of points, related by a projection, have the same ordering, then their cross ratio will be preserved.
concepts.motivation_md: Because the cross-ratio formula is not symmetric for all permutations, maintaining consistent point ordering is crucial for the invariance property to hold during calculations.
concepts.recap_md:
- There are 24 possible orderings of four points, yielding six distinct cross-ratio values.
- Invariance is preserved only if the ordering remains consistent between the two sets of points.

concepts.title: Height Measurement using Parallel Lines
concepts.one_liner: Relative heights in an image can be estimated by projecting objects onto a common reference line and applying the cross-ratio invariant.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Given the height of a reference object, the location of the horizon line and one vanishing point, how can we estimate the height of other objects in the scene?)

Due to perspective projection, we cannot directly compare the relative height of objects (like a desk and a bookshelf) using distances measured over the image. To compare 3D distances using 2D image distances, objects must be put in correspondence. For example, the bookshelf height is defined by the 2D locations of its bottom $\mathbf{g}_b$ and top $\mathbf{t}_b$, while the desk height is defined by $\mathbf{g}_d$ and $\mathbf{t}_d$. To use image distances, we first translate the points defining the desk height onto the bookshelf and then use the cross-ratio invariant.

Using homogeneous coordinates for image vectors, the steps are:
- Estimate the ground line $\boldsymbol{l}_1 = \mathbf{g}_d \times \mathbf{g}_b$.
- Compute the vanishing point $\mathbf{a} = \boldsymbol{l}_1 \times \mathbf{h}$ where $\mathbf{h}$ is the horizon line.
- Compute the line $\boldsymbol{l}_2 = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{t}_d$ passing through the vanishing point and the top of the desk.
- Find the intersection $\mathbf{b}$ of $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ with the bookshelf line $\boldsymbol{l}_3 = \mathbf{g}_b \times \mathbf{t}_b$, calculated as $\mathbf{b} = \boldsymbol{l}_2 \times \boldsymbol{l}_3$.

This can be expressed in a single equation:
$$\mathbf{b} = (((\mathbf{g}_d \times \mathbf{g}_b) \times \mathbf{h}) \times \mathbf{t}_d) \times (\mathbf{g}_b \times \mathbf{t}_b)$$
concepts.motivation_md: Perspective distortion makes direct measurement impossible. This technique provides a geometric way to 'transfer' the height of one object to the location of another, enabling comparison through the cross-ratio.
concepts.recap_md:
- Direct image distance comparison is invalid for 3D heights due to perspective.
- Objects are related by projecting heights onto a common reference line using vanishing points and the horizon.

- Objects are related by projecting heights onto a common reference line using vanishing points and the horizon.

concepts.title: Projective Invariants
concepts.one_liner: Projective invariants are geometric measures that remain unchanged after a perspective projection.
concepts.content: Projective invariants are measures that do not change after perspective projection. The cross-ratio is the most important projective invariant.
concepts.motivation_md: Invariants are the 'holy grail' of computer vision because they allow us to identify properties of the 3D world that are not destroyed by the process of taking a photograph.
concepts.recap_md:
- Projective invariants are properties unaffected by perspective projection.
- The cross-ratio is the primary example of such an invariant.

concepts.title: Height Propagation to Supported Objects
concepts.one_liner: Heights of objects not on the ground can be estimated by propagating height information from their supporting surfaces.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Estimating the height of the red bottle. For an object not in the ground we can propagate information from the objects that support it.)

For an object not on the ground, such as a bottle on a desk, we can estimate its height by propagating information from the objects that support it. To project the bottle height onto a reference line (like the corner of a bookshelf), we find two vertically aligned parallel 3D lines. The first line, $\boldsymbol{l}_1$, connects the bottom of the bottle $\mathbf{g}_e$ and the point $\mathbf{b}$ (the top of the desk projected onto the bookshelf). These points are at the same height. The intersection of $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ with the horizon line $\mathbf{h}$ gives the vanishing point $\mathbf{a}$. Connecting $\mathbf{a}$ with the top of the bottle $\mathbf{t}_e$ gives the second line $\boldsymbol{l}_2$. The intersection of $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ with the reference bookshelf line is point $\mathbf{c}$. The distance between $\mathbf{c}$ and the ground in 3D represents the sum of the bookshelf and desk heights.

The compact equation is:
$$\mathbf{c} = (((\mathbf{g}_e \times \mathbf{b}) \times \mathbf{h}) \times \mathbf{t}_e) \times (\mathbf{g}_b \times \mathbf{t}_b)$$
Note that this calculation requires $\mathbf{b}$ to be computed first.
concepts.motivation_md: Many objects in a scene do not rest on the ground plane. This technique extends height measurement to stacked or supported objects by chaining geometric projections.
concepts.recap_md:
- Height information can be propagated from supporting objects to supported ones.
- The technique uses parallel lines and vanishing points to transfer heights to a reference vertical line.

slots.key_passage:

- The technique uses parallel lines and vanishing points to transfer heights to a reference vertical line.

concepts.title: Calibration of the Projected World Axis
concepts.one_liner: The cross-ratio is used to calibrate the projection of world coordinate axes in the image plane using vanishing points and a reference measure.
concepts.content:
Let's start assuming we know the location of some arbitrary 3D distance to the origin on each axis that we will denote by $\alpha_X$, $\alpha_Y$ and $\alpha_Z$. The question is, where do we place the ticks for $k\alpha_X$, $k\alpha_Y$ and $k\alpha_Z$ for all $k$? We will use the cross-ratio to calibrate the projection of the world coordinate system in the image plane. For doing this we will need the location of the horizon line of a reference plane (i.e. the ground plane), the position of the orthogonal vanishing point and the real measure of one object in the scene.

As shown in (see figure: Using the cross-ratio invariant to project the world coordinates into the image using only the vanishing points.) (a) we can use the cross-ratio to estimate the location of the points $Y= k \alpha_X$ where $\alpha_X$ is an arbitrary constant as shown in (see figure: Using the cross-ratio invariant to project the world coordinates into the image using only the vanishing points.) (b), and the corresponding image location $r$, for $k=1$, is chosen arbitrarily as shown in (see figure: Using the cross-ratio invariant to project the world coordinates into the image using only the vanishing points.) (a). Due to perspective projection, the image projection of the point $Y= k \alpha_X$ will not be evenly spaced in the image. In this particular example we chose the orientation of the world axis in image coordinates to be aligned with the location of the vanishing points.
concepts.motivation_md: To measure distances in a single image, one must first establish a metric scale on the projected world axes. This technique allows for the creation of a 'virtual ruler' along the axes despite perspective distortion.
concepts.recap_md: - Use the cross-ratio invariant to determine the spacing of coordinate ticks in a perspective view.

concepts.title: Locating a 3D Point using Context
concepts.one_liner: Contextual information, such as object contact with the ground and vanishing points, allows for the recovery of a point's 3D location from a single image.
concepts.content:
In the absence of any other information, we can not recover the 3D location of a single point $\mathbf{P}$ from a single view as illustrated in (see figure: Figure (a) In the absence of any other information, we can not recover the 3D location of point $\mathbf{P}$. (b) If we are given a way to project the point P into the ground, then we can read out...) [a]. But real world scenes are composed by a multitude of objects providing context, which allows solving the 3D estimation problem even with just a single image. In the previous section we showed how to estimate the height of an object, here we show how to estimated the 3D coordinates of a point.

The basic procedure is illustrated in (see figure: Figure (a) In the absence of any other information, we can not recover the 3D location of point $\mathbf{P}$. (b) If we are given a way to project the point P into the ground, then we can read out...) [b]. The trick consists in using context (what object is the point part of, where is the horizon line of the scene and where are the vanishing points) to estimate 3D from a single image. It suffices to know that the point $\mathbf{P}$ belongs to an object that is in contact with the ground and the geometry of this object provides the information to localize the projection of the point $\mathbf{P}$ on the ground plane, which we denote with $\mathbf{G}$.
concepts.motivation_md: A single 2D point is inherently ambiguous in 3D space. By using environmental context like the ground plane and vanishing points, we can constrain the point's position and recover its full 3D coordinates.

concepts.title: Technique for Locating a 3D Point
concepts.one_liner: 3D coordinates are estimated by projecting a point onto the ground plane and then intersecting lines with the calibrated world-coordinate axes.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Figure (a) In the absence of any other information, we can not recover the 3D location of point $\mathbf{P}$. (b) If we are given a way to project the point P into the ground, then we can read out...)

Once we know the image location of the projection of the 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ to the ground, $\mathbf{G}$, we can project this point to the world-coordinate axis. To estimate the $Y$-coordinate we use a similar method as the one described in the previous section. We first find the line, $\boldsymbol{l}_3$, that passes by the point $\mathbf{G}$ and the origin, and then find the intersection with the horizon line, giving the point $\mathbf{v}$. Next, find the line, $\boldsymbol{l}_4$, that passes by $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{P}$. The intersection of $\boldsymbol{l}_4$ with the $Y_w$-axis gives the coordinate $P_y$. The $P_x$ and $P_z$ coordinates can be obtained by connecting $\mathbf{G}$ with the vanishing points $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique provides a geometric algorithm to extract numerical 3D coordinates from a 2D image once the scene's horizon and axes are calibrated.
concepts.recap_md: - Project the point to the ground plane $\mathbf{G}$ and then to the world-coordinate axes.

concepts.title: Reference Planes for 3D Recovery
concepts.one_liner: 3D recovery techniques can be applied using any plane with a known horizon line as a reference, not just the ground plane.
concepts.content: Here we have been using the ground plane as a reference. But the same idea can be applied if we know the projection of the point $\mathbf{P}$ into another plane with a known horizon line.
concepts.motivation_md: In many scenes, the ground might be obscured or the point of interest might be related to a wall or table; this concept generalizes 3D recovery to any known planar surface.
concepts.recap_md: - Any plane with a known horizon line can serve as a reference for 3D point recovery.

concepts.title: Camera Calibration from Vanishing Points
concepts.one_liner: Camera intrinsic parameters can be extracted by using the geometric constraints provided by three orthogonal vanishing points.
concepts.content:
In the previous chapters, we have seen different methods to calibrate a camera. We saw that we could do it by taking pictures of a calibration pattern, and we also showed that we can extract both the intrinsics and extrinsics from a set of 3D points and their image correspondences. Here we will see a different method that uses only the vanishing points to extract the camera parameters; note that this method will only work under some conditions.

The first step consists in finding the vanishing points in the image. Let's use the office picture from @fig-vanishing_lines. In this particular scene there are many parallel lines in 3D, and they also happen to be parallel to the three directions we used to define the world coordinates system. Therefore, the three vanishing points are also aligned with the world coordinate axis.

Let's assume that we have three orthogonal vanishing directions. That is the vectors $\mathbf{D}_1$, $\mathbf{D}_2$, and $\mathbf{D}_3$ are orthogonal in 3D. From equation (@eq-vanishing_projection), the vanishing points measured on the image are the result of projecting $\mathbf{D}_1$, $\mathbf{D}_2$, and $\mathbf{D}_3$ into the image using the unknown camera projection matrix. We will use the vanishing points to derive a set of constraints on the projection matrix. To do this, we start by inverting equation (@eq-vanishing_projection):
$$\mathbf{D}_i = \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_i$$
Because the vectors $\mathbf{D}_i$ are orthogonal, we have that $\mathbf{D}_i^{\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{D}_j = 0$ for $i \neq j$. Therefore, we can write:
$$\mathbf{D}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{D}_j = \mathbf{v}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{R}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_j $$
As $\mathbf{R}$ is an orthonormal matrix, we have that $\mathbf{R}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{R}^{-1} = \mathbf{I}$, resulting in a relationship that only depends on the intrinsic camera parameters $\mathbf{K}$:
$$\mathbf{D}_i^T \mathbf{D}_j = \mathbf{v}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{v}_j = 0$$
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional calibration requires physical patterns. This method allows for 'auto-calibration' using only the natural geometry of a scene (like the corners of a room), provided there are three mutually orthogonal directions.
concepts.recap_md: - Orthogonal vanishing directions in 3D provide constraints on the intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$.

concepts.title: Conic Matrix
concepts.one_liner: The conic matrix $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$ is a fundamental matrix used to relate vanishing points to camera intrinsics.
concepts.content:
It is useful to define the following matrix:
$$\mathbf{W} =  \mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$$
This is also known as the **conic matrix** and it has lots of different properties.
concepts.motivation_md: The conic matrix (often related to the Image of the Absolute Conic) simplifies the equations for camera calibration by encapsulating the intrinsic parameters into a single symmetric matrix.
concepts.recap_md: - Defined as $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{K}^{-\mathsf{T}} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$.

concepts.title: Linear Constraints on the Conic Matrix
concepts.one_liner: If the camera's skew parameter is zero, the conic matrix $\mathbf{W}$ has a specific structure that allows for linear constraints based on vanishing points.
concepts.content: If we assume that the skew parameter of the intrinsic camera matrix is zero, then the matrix $\mathbf{W}$ has a very particular structure and it has only four different values: $$\mathbf{W} = \begin{bmatrix} a & 0 & b\\ 0 & a & c\\ b & c & d \end{bmatrix}$$ Using the vanishing projection constraint, we can derive a linear constraint on the values $a,b,c,d$ for each pair of vanishing points. Defining the vector $\mathbf{w}=[a~b~c~d]^\mathsf{T}$, we can rewrite the vanishing projection constraint into a system of linear equations that has the form: $$\mathbf{A} \mathbf{w} = 0$$
concepts.motivation_md: This technique simplifies the process of camera calibration by reducing the number of unknown parameters in the conic matrix, allowing it to be solved using linear methods when vanishing points are known.
concepts.recap_md:
- Zero skew reduces the conic matrix $\mathbf{W}$ to four unique parameters: $a, b, c, d$.
 - Each pair of vanishing points provides a linear constraint on these parameters.
 - The resulting system of equations takes the form $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w} = 0$.

concepts.title: Solving for Camera Parameters using Vanishing Points
concepts.one_liner: Camera parameters can be recovered by solving a linear system via SVD and performing Cholesky factorization on the resulting conic matrix.
concepts.content: The linear equation can be solved with the singular value decomposition (SVD) and the result is the eigenvector with the smallest eigenvalue. Once we have $\mathbf{W}$, we can find the intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ by using the Cholesky factorization, which decomposes a matrix as the product of an upper triangular matrix and its transpose. The last step is to normalize the result by normalizing all the matrix values so that the value on the bottom-right side is 1.
concepts.motivation_md: Once linear constraints are established, this method provides a robust numerical procedure to extract the actual intrinsic camera matrix from the conic representation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Solve the linear system $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w}=0$ using SVD to find the conic matrix $\mathbf{W}$.
 - Use Cholesky factorization on $\mathbf{W}$ to recover the upper triangular intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$.
 - Normalize the final matrix so the bottom-right entry is 1.

concepts.title: Linear Perspective
concepts.one_liner: Linear perspective is a technique that uses parallel lines and vanishing points to infer 3D scene structure from 2D images.
concepts.content: Linear perspective uses parallel and orthogonal lines, vanishing points, the ground plane, and the horizon line to infer the 3D scene structure from a 2D image. The discovery of linear perspective is attributed to the Italian architect Filippo Brunelleschi in 1415. Linear perspective relies on specific assumptions about the scene; consequently, it is not a general cue useful in all scenes, but it is very powerful in most human-made environments.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear perspective provides a geometric framework for understanding how 3D depth is projected onto a 2D plane, which is essential for both realistic art and computer vision algorithms.
concepts.recap_md:
- It utilizes geometric features like vanishing points and horizon lines to recover 3D information.
 - The technique is particularly effective in man-made environments with many parallel and orthogonal lines.
 - It was historically pioneered by Filippo Brunelleschi during the Renaissance.

concepts.title: Leaning Tower Visual Illusion
concepts.one_liner: The leaning tower illusion occurs when the brain interprets identical side-by-side images as having different tilts because their parallel lines do not converge to a single vanishing point.
concepts.content: The human visual system makes use of vanishing points for 3D perception, which can lead to the leaning tower visual illusion. In this illusion, a pair of identical images of the Leaning Tower of Pisa are placed side by side. Despite being identical, they create an illusion of leaning with different angles, where the image on the right appears to have a greater tilt. One explanation is that the lines of each tower converge at a different vanishing point. If both towers were parallel in 3D, all the lines would converge to the same 2D vanishing point. Because they do not, our brain automatically interprets that the towers should have different 3D orientations. (see figure: The *leaning tower illusion* @Kingdom2017 involves two identical pictures placed side by side. The picture on the right appears to be more tilted than the one on the left.)
concepts.motivation_md: This illusion demonstrates how deeply the human brain relies on the geometry of vanishing points to reconstruct 3D scenes, even when that logic leads to an incorrect perception.
concepts.recap_md:
- Identical side-by-side images of a tower appear to tilt at different angles.
 - The illusion stems from the brain's automatic processing of vanishing points for 3D depth.
 - It highlights that our perception of orientation is relative to expected convergence points in a scene.

concepts.title: Vanishing Points in Homogeneous Coordinates
concepts.one_liner: In homogeneous coordinates, a vanishing point is the projection of a point at infinity, represented by a finite vector where the last coordinate is zero.
concepts.content: Homogeneous coordinates allow us to represent points at infinity with finite coordinates by setting the last element to 0. A 3D line can be written in parametric vector form as: $$\mathbf{P}_t = \begin{bmatrix} X_0 + t D_X\\ Y_0 + t D_Y\\ Z_0 + t D_Z\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} X_0/t + D_X\\ Y_0 /t+ D_Y\\ Z_0/t + D_Z\\ 1/t \end{bmatrix}$$ In the limit $t \to \infty$, the fourth coordinate converges to 0, resulting in: $$\mathbf{P}_\infty = \begin{bmatrix} D_X\\ D_Y\\ D_Z\\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{D}\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ The vanishing point in homogeneous coordinates is the projection of $\mathbf{P}_\infty$ using the camera model $\mathbf{M}$: $$\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{P}_\infty = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{T} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{D}\\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{D}$$ This shows that vanishing point coordinates do not depend on camera translation $\mathbf{T}$, only on rotation $\mathbf{R}$ and intrinsics $\mathbf{K}$. If a scene is captured by two identical cameras translated from each other, their corresponding images will have the same vanishing points. If parallel projection is used instead of perspective projection, all vanishing points project at infinity in the image plane.
concepts.motivation_md: Using homogeneous coordinates simplifies the math of perspective projection by treating points at infinity (vanishing points) as standard vectors, making calculations for rotation and projection more elegant.
concepts.recap_md:
- Points at infinity are represented in homogeneous coordinates by a zero in the final coordinate.
 - Vanishing points are invariant to camera translation and depend only on camera rotation and intrinsics.
 - The vanishing point $\mathbf{v}$ is calculated as the product $\mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{D}$, where $\mathbf{D}$ is the direction of the 3D lines.
